title: Managing a stage boundary: practices applied and judging the process
blurb: Name the practice a stage boundary action applies, and judge whether the boundary gives the board what it needs to decide.
question: At the end of a stage, the project manager plans the next stage but leaves the business case untouched because benefits come after the project. Entries and sponsorship are below forecast. Is the stage boundary handled effectively, and why?

teach.h: Two question types on the stage boundary
teach.body: Practitioner papers ask which practice a stage boundary action applies, using table 18.3, and whether the boundary is handled effectively. The test for effectiveness is simple: does the board end up with what it needs to review the stage, approve the next stage or exception plan, and confirm the project is still justified with acceptable risks? Check the action against the objectives in 18.2 and pick the reason that explains it.

teach.h: How the stage boundary applies the practices
head: Practice
What happens at the boundary
rows: End stage report created and issued (table 18.3)
Team performance, health and well-being reviewed for lessons and the end stage report (table 18.3)
Issue register reviewed: stage issues closed, next-stage ones added; issue MA reviewed (table 18.3)
Quality register checked for the stage's quality activities (table 18.3)
Next stage or exception plan prepared; project plan updated (activities)
Business case updated with costs, benefits and risk exposure (activities)
teach.caption: The first four rows paraphrase the official table 18.3 extracts; the last two come straight from the activities themselves.

root.label: What did the PM review or produce?

teach.caption: Reviewing team health and well-being is ORGANIZING, even though it feeds lessons and the end stage report.

teach.body: An effective boundary assures the board that every product in the current stage plan is complete and approved, prepares the next stage plan (or exception plan), reviews and if needed updates the PID, gives the board what it needs to judge continuing viability, records lessons, and asks for authorization. If the business case is no longer justified, a board decision to stop is a sound result of the boundary, not a failure.

rows.label: Business case
values: Left as it was at initiation

rows.label: Team
values: Not reviewed after a hard stage

teach.h: A business case trigger at Carrowford
teach.caption: Entries finish June below the trigger, so the festival is reduced. The boundary must carry that change into the business case.

teach.body: As the build-up stage ends, project manager Kezia Oduya checks the quality register shows the safety plan review and volunteer training sign-offs were done (quality). She closes resolved issues and carries event-week ones forward (issues), reviews the well-being of volunteer coordinators after a demanding stage (organizing), and updates the business case: entries reached 5,600, so the festival is reduced and the local spending forecast falls. Her end stage report (progress) lets the board decide on event week with current facts.

teach.text: Traps: (1) Reviewing team health and well-being applies ORGANIZING, not progress. (2) The business case is updated at EVERY boundary, even when benefits will be measured after closure. (3) Asking for the next stage while a current-stage product is still unapproved, without telling the board, fails the boundary's first objective. (4) A board decision to stop at a boundary is not a failure when justification has gone.

items: Table 18.3: progress (end stage report), organizing (team performance and well-being), issues (issue register and MA), quality (quality register).
Plans and business case are applied through the planning and update activities.
Judge against 18.2: products complete and approved, plans ready, PID reviewed, viability shown, lessons recorded, authorization requested.
Disclose concessions and gaps; the board decides on facts, and may stop.

summary: You can now name the practice behind any managing a stage boundary action, using table 18.3 and the activities. You can also judge whether a boundary gives the board what it needs, and pick the reason that explains it.

A.q: Carrowford City Council is delivering its first half marathon and festival. As the build-up stage ends, project manager Kezia Oduya reviews how the volunteer coordinators and Paceline's race team performed and how their health and well-being held up over a demanding stage, and feeds the findings into lessons and the end stage report. Which practice is the 'managing a stage boundary' process applying?
options: Progress
Organizing
Quality
Business case
A.why: Table 18.3: the organizing practice is applied when project team performance, health and well-being are reviewed for input to lessons and the end stage report.

whyNot.0: Progress is applied by creating and issuing the end stage report; the review of the team itself applies organizing.
whyNot.2: Quality is applied by checking the quality register for the stage's quality activities.
whyNot.3: The business case is applied when it is updated with revised forecasts; reviewing the team applies organizing.

A.q: At the end of the Carrowford build-up stage, Kezia Oduya checks the quality register to confirm that the stage's quality activities, such as the review of the event safety plan and the volunteer training sign-offs, were all carried out. Which practice is the 'managing a stage boundary' process applying?
options: Plans
Issues
Progress
Quality
A.why: Table 18.3: the quality practice is applied when the quality register is checked to confirm the stage's quality activities have been performed.

whyNot.0: Plans is applied through the next stage plan and project plan updates.
whyNot.1: Issues is applied through the issue register and issue management approach.
whyNot.2: Progress is applied through the end stage report.

A.q: At the end of the Carrowford build-up stage, Kezia Oduya reviews the issue register, closes the issues resolved during the stage, adds those that need action in event week, and checks whether the issue management approach needs changing. Which practice is the 'managing a stage boundary' process applying?
options: Issues
Risk
Plans
Organizing
A.why: Table 18.3: the issues practice is applied when the issue register is reviewed to close the stage's issues and add next-stage ones, and the issue management approach is reviewed.

whyNot.1: Risk would be applied through the risk register and risk management approach; this action concerns issues.
whyNot.2: Plans is applied through the next stage plan and project plan.
whyNot.3: Organizing is applied through the review of team performance and well-being.

B.q: At the end of the Carrowford build-up stage, Kezia Oduya creates the end stage report, summarizing the stage's performance and the overall project position, and issues it to the project board. Which practice is the 'managing a stage boundary' process applying?
options: Plans
Business case
Progress
Organizing
B.why: Table 18.3: the progress practice is applied when the end stage report is created and issued.

whyNot.0: Plans is applied by preparing the next stage plan and updating the project plan.
whyNot.1: The end stage report draws on the updated business case, but creating the report applies progress.
whyNot.3: Organizing is applied by reviewing team performance and well-being.

B.q: Earlier in the Carrowford build-up stage, approval of the event safety plan was forecast to be late. After Kezia Oduya's exception report, the board asked her for an exception plan. Which statement about the end stage report is correct while she prepares the exception plan?
options: She prepares an end stage report with every exception plan
She prepares an end stage report if the board requires one
She replaces the end stage report with a highlight report
She asks Paceline's race director to write the report
B.why: When an exception plan is prepared, an end stage report is produced only if the board requires one.

whyNot.0: With an exception plan, the end stage report is not automatic; it is prepared only when the board requires it.
whyNot.2: A highlight report is the routine controlling a stage report, not a substitute at a boundary.
whyNot.3: The PM is responsible for the end stage report; a team manager is consulted.

B.q: Race entries reached 5,600 by the end of June, below the 6,000 trigger, so the Carrowford riverside festival is being reduced and the forecast of local spending falls. At the end of the stage, Kezia Oduya revises the business case to reflect the lower forecast. Which practice is the 'managing a stage boundary' process applying?
options: The progress practice
The risk practice
The organizing practice
The business case practice
B.why: Updating the business case with revised forecasts at the boundary applies the business case practice, keeping continued business justification under review for the board.

whyNot.0: Progress is applied by the end stage report, which uses the updated business case but does not revise it.
whyNot.1: The update may include aggregated risk exposure, but revising the business case applies the business case practice.
whyNot.2: Organizing is applied at the boundary by reviewing team performance and well-being, not by revising forecasts.

C.q: At the end of the Carrowford build-up stage, Kezia Oduya prepares the plan for event week but leaves the business case unchanged, saying the economic benefits can only be measured after the race. Entries are below forecast and sponsorship income has fallen. Is the stage boundary being handled effectively, and why?
options: Yes, because benefits are measured after the event has closed
Yes, because the business case is next updated in closing
No, because the benefits approach has replaced the business case
No, because the board needs it to confirm continued justification
C.why: The boundary must give the board what it needs to confirm the project is still justified; update the business case reflects changes in costs, income and benefit forecasts (18.1, 18.2).

whyNot.0: Benefits may be measured after the event, but forecasts still need updating so the board can decide whether to continue.
whyNot.1: The business case is updated in closing too, but that does not remove the need to update it at each boundary.
whyNot.2: The benefits management approach supports the business case; it does not replace it.

C.q: The Carrowford team of council staff and volunteer coordinators worked long hours during the build-up stage. At the stage boundary, Kezia Oduya decides not to review team performance and well-being, because the stage finished within its tolerances. Is the stage boundary being handled effectively, and why?
options: Yes, because the stage finished within its agreed tolerances
Yes, because team well-being is reviewed when the project closes
No, because the review feeds lessons and the end stage report
No, because well-being must be covered in every highlight report
C.why: Table 18.3: at the boundary, team performance, health and well-being are reviewed for input to lessons and the end stage report. Skipping it after a demanding stage loses those lessons before event week.

whyNot.0: Being within tolerance is good news, but it does not explain dropping the review of team well-being.
whyNot.1: Closing a project also reviews the team, but that is too late to act on lessons before event week.
whyNot.3: Highlight reports cover stage status; the well-being review that feeds lessons is a boundary action.

C.q: Kezia Oduya asks the Carrowford board to authorize the final stage, although the event safety plan, a product in the build-up stage plan, has not yet been approved. She does not mention this in her briefing. Is this an appropriate application of managing a stage boundary, and why?
options: Yes, because the approval can be tracked as a risk in event week
Yes, because the board can grant a concession in directing a project
No, because the board should be assured all stage products are approved
No, because the missing approval should go into an exception plan
C.why: An objective of managing a stage boundary is to assure the board that all products in the current stage plan are complete and approved (18.2). Hiding an unapproved product denies the board a fair decision.

whyNot.0: Tracking it as a risk does not excuse hiding from the board that a stage product is unapproved.
whyNot.1: The board might accept a concession, but only if the PM tells it about the gap.
whyNot.3: An exception plan follows a board request after an exception report; the failing here is not disclosing the gap.

reteach.title: The boundary as a health check
reteach.question: If the stage boundary is a health check before the board signs off the next stage, what does each practice check?

blocks.h: Six checks before the board decides
blocks.body: Quality: were the stage's quality activities done? Issues: are stage issues closed or carried forward? Organizing: how is the team performing and coping? Plans: is the next stage planned and the project plan current? Business case: is the project still worth it? Progress: is it all summarized in the end stage report?

blocks.text: A boundary is effective when the board decides on full, honest information. Hidden gaps, an un-updated business case or a skipped team review all fail it.

explain.h: Progress and organizing at the boundary
explain.body: Progress: the end stage report is created and issued. Organizing: team performance, health and well-being are reviewed, and the findings feed lessons and the end stage report.

test.q: After reviewing how tired the volunteer coordinators became during the build-up stage, Kezia Oduya records lessons about rotas for future events and notes the findings in her end stage report. Which practice does table 18.3 link the review to?
options: Progress
Organizing
Quality
Business case
test.why: Table 18.3 links reviewing project team performance, health and well-being for lessons and the end stage report to the organizing practice.

whyNot.0: Progress is linked to creating and issuing the end stage report, not to reviewing the team.
whyNot.2: Quality is linked to checking the quality register.
whyNot.3: The business case is updated at the boundary, but table 18.3 links the team review to organizing.

explain.h: Issues and quality at the boundary
explain.body: Issues: the issue register is reviewed to close the stage's issues and add those for the next stage, and the issue management approach is reviewed. Quality: the quality register is checked to confirm the stage's quality activities were performed.

test.q: Bernadette Lowe of internal audit, who provides project assurance, asks Kezia Oduya which boundary action applies the quality practice. Which action does?
options: Checking the quality register for the stage's activities
Reviewing the issue register and closing the stage's issues
Creating the end stage report and issuing it to the board
Reviewing the team's performance, health and well-being
test.why: Table 18.3: the quality practice is applied at the boundary by checking the quality register for the stage's quality activities.

whyNot.1: Reviewing the issue register applies the issues practice.
whyNot.2: Creating and issuing the end stage report applies the progress practice.
whyNot.3: Reviewing team performance and well-being applies the organizing practice.

explain.h: Judging plans and the business case
explain.body: A boundary is only useful if the board can judge continuing viability. That needs the next stage planned, the project plan updated with actuals and forecasts, and the business case revised for changed costs, income, benefits and risk exposure.

test.q: Andrew Mallory, executive for the Carrowford event, wants to know whether the project is still worth continuing before event week. Which boundary action best supports that decision?
options: Sending the board the last highlight report of the stage
Asking Paceline for its latest checkpoint reports
Updating the business case with revised income and benefits
Recording the course certificate in the product register
test.why: Updating the business case with current costs, income and benefit forecasts is what lets the board confirm continued business justification at the boundary (18.1).

whyNot.0: The highlight report is a routine stage report; the viability decision needs the updated business case.
whyNot.1: Checkpoint reports go to the PM and describe work package status, not the project's viability.
whyNot.3: Updating the product register records product status; it does not show whether the project is still worth doing.

explain.body: The boundary ends with the PM asking the board to proceed. The board may approve the next stage, ask for changes, or stop the project. Stopping because the business case is no longer justified is a sound outcome, not a failure.

test.q: Suppose the Carrowford board, after reviewing the end stage report and updated business case, concludes the event is no longer justified and decides to close the project early. How should this decision be viewed?
options: As a failure of the project management team
As a sound decision now justification has gone
As a breach the PM must report as an exception
As a decision the PM should have made earlier
test.why: Managing a stage boundary gives the board the chance to stop a project that is no longer justified; doing so is not a failure (ch 18).

whyNot.0: Stopping an unjustified project is the control working as intended, not a failure.
whyNot.2: The board is making a decision at a control point; no exception report is needed for it.
whyNot.3: Premature closure is triggered by the project board, not decided by the PM.
